declared_equivalent_mutants.reason: swap_boolean_condition at redirect.py:29:7 changes `if not parsed.scheme and not parsed.netloc:` to `if not parsed.scheme or not parsed.netloc:` (And -> Or). By the time this line runs, target has already passed the line-18 non-empty-string guard and the line-23 `target.startswith("//")` guard. Given urlparse's grammar, a non-empty netloc can only ever be produced from a scheme-less input by a literal '//' prefix (RFC 3986 authority component requires the '//' marker), and any such input was already rejected at line 23 -- so at line 29, `scheme == ''` implies `netloc == ''` for every surviving input, making the AND and OR conditions identical (both True) whenever scheme is empty. The two conditions can only diverge when scheme is non-empty and netloc is empty (AND is False, OR is True) -- e.g. 'javascript:alert(1)', 'mailto:x@y', 'ftp:foo'. For every such input, urlparse's scheme grammar (ALPHA (ALPHA|DIGIT|+|-|.)*) requires the first character to be alphabetic, so target can never start with '/' when scheme is non-empty. The mutant's newly-entered branch therefore always evaluates `target.startswith("/")` as False and falls through to `raise ValueError("... must be an absolute path")`, while the reference (skipping this branch for the same input) proceeds to line 39's scheme check and raises ValueError there instead (either 'scheme not allowed', or -- for an allowed scheme with no netloc, e.g. 'http:foo' -- 'must have a host' at line 43). Both versions raise ValueError for every input in this class; only the message/line differs, which the contract never specifies. Verified empirically by reconstructing the exact mutant and diffing accept/reject outcome AND exception type against the reference over 60+ probe inputs (all string edge cases: multi-slash, colon-only, scheme-with-empty-netloc, non-string types, case variants, userinfo tricks) -- zero observable differences found, consistent with the proof above.

This line is only reached after line 39 has confirmed `parsed.scheme in ("http", "https")`. urlparse's `.hostname` property is derived from `.netloc` and is documented/implemented to return None whenever netloc is empty -- there is no input for which netloc is empty but hostname is non-None. So when this guard's condition is True (netloc empty) and its raise is skipped, execution falls through to line 47: `if parsed.hostname != allowed_host:`, which evaluates `None != allowed_host`. `allowed_host` is a trusted configuration parameter supplied by the calling application (not part of the adversarial `target` input space the task contract defends against) and is always a non-empty hostname string in every case the contract or its hidden/regression suites exercise (e.g. "app.example.com"), so `None != allowed_host` is always True, and the mutant raises ValueError('... does not match allowed host ...') instead of ValueError('... must have a host'). Both are ValueError, for every reachable input (e.g. 'http:foo', 'http:/foo', 'http://', 'https:'), just with a different (contract-unspecified) message. Verified empirically: reconstructed the exact mutant and diffed against the reference over the same 60+ probe input set with allowed_host fixed to a realistic non-empty value -- zero differences in accept/reject outcome or exception type.
